rows.quizPrompt: What is the transition dipole moment, why does its value decide whether a spectroscopic line is bright or dark, and what makes it vanish?
rows.answer: The transition dipole moment is mu_fi = <f|mu-hat|i>, the matrix element of the dipole operator between the initial and final quantum states - physically, how much the molecule's charge distribution shifts as it changes state. Because light couples to a molecule through V = -mu-hat . E, Fermi's golden rule makes the transition rate (and hence the absorption/emission intensity) proportional to |mu_fi|^2. So a large transition dipole gives a bright line and a fast radiative decay, while mu_fi = 0 makes the electric-dipole transition forbidden - absent or very faint. What makes it vanish is symmetry: the integral <f|mu-hat|i> over all space is zero unless the combined symmetry of the two states and the dipole operator is totally symmetric (equivalently, the charge rearrangement has a net direction). This gives the standard selection rules - Delta-v = +/-1 for a harmonic vibration, Delta-l = +/-1 (Laporte) for atomic electronic transitions, Delta-J = +/-1 for a rigid rotor. Forbidden transitions still appear faintly through vibronic, spin-orbit, or magnetic-dipole leakage.
